items.t: The Last Mile to the Real World: Agent-Native Primitives as Reusable Building Blocks for Solving Real-World Tasks

We propose Debate-to-Deceive (D2D), a multi-agent debate framework grounde…
items.sm: Debate-to-Deceive uses competing LLM agents to evolve rhetorical strategies and generate adversarial passages intended to manipulate automated fact-checking judgments.

items.t: s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL

We introduce MCPHallu, a…

Prior work has studied deception under goal conflicts and the leakage of private information, but largely as separate problems. We stu…

items.t: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
items.a: Allan Grosvenor, Anton Zemlyansky, Abdul Wahab, Kyrylo Bohachov, Aras Dogan, Ryland Adams, Dwyer Deighan
items.x: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated phys…
items.sm: Introduces GURU, an agent system where learned models propose actions, symbolic rules enforce limits, and validated physics determines acceptable outcomes.

items.t: Architecting Fairness-Aware LLM Interactions
items.a: Alessandra Parziale, Valeria Pontillo, Fabio Palomba, Patrizio Pelliccione
items.x: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools but may generate stereotypical, discriminatory, or unfair responses. As LLMs become embedded in decision-critical software systems, fairness can no longer be treated as a downstream evaluation step, but must become an architectural concern of the interaction itself. Yet current fairness approaches operate as standalone evaluation techniques,…
items.sm: Proposes an agent architecture that checks and revises language model responses for fairness violations before delivering them.

items.t: MAPLE: A Multimodal Mobile Agent with Playbook-Learned Experience
items.a: Jun Wang, Aurora Wei, Lucas Spangher, Ming Zhang, Eugene Ie, Yiannis Kantaros
items.x: Autonomous agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) show great potential in navigating mobile graphical user interfaces (GUIs) to complete complex tasks. However, existing paradigms face fundamental scalability bottlenecks: fine-tuning requires massive high-fidelity datasets or prohibitive training time and compute, while gradient-free approaches rely on custom static heuristics or costly trial-and-error traje…
items.sm: Introduces MAPLE, a mobile interface agent framework that shares experience between agents and updates prompts during execution without retraining models.

items.t: Latent-Lens: Visual Perception in Small Language Models Through Latent Communication
items.a: Mo Shahdloo, Faegheh Sardari, Mathew Salvaris
items.x: Bridging independent vision-language models (VLMs) and small language models (SLMs) in a modular multi-agent system typically forces them to exchange information as discrete text, which creates a lossy bottleneck for spatial and fine-grained details. This constraint is especially acute for SLMs, whose limited capacity makes them more reliant on the quality of the input signal. Recent latent-communication methods exch…
items.sm: Introduces a lightweight adapter that transfers visual information directly between a frozen vision language model and a frozen small language model through hidden representations.

items.t: Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications
items.a: Hanqi Sun, Yuchen Shao, Hanyi Si, Beibei Xu, Lisheng Wang, Chengcheng Wan
items.x: LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) applications can produce useful intermediate results while leaving task requirements unsatisfied. Repairing such executions requires identifying the work still needed and the completed results that can support it. We present \tool, a contribution-guided runtime repair framework for MAS applications. \tool derives expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirement…
items.sm: Introduces Dittany, which repairs incomplete agent workflows by identifying unmet requirements, preserving validated results, and revising actions or dependencies.

items.a: Rishabh Mediratta, Lingyun Xiao, Peter Stone, Joydeep Biswas, Elias Stengel-Eskin
items.x: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both compl…
items.sm: Introduces ParallACT, a benchmark studying how coding agents coordinate complementary or conflicting requests in shared repositories without a central orchestrator.

items.t: Ask on Demand: Targeted Peer Communication for Parallel Agentic Systems
items.a: Haofu Yang, Hongyang Yin, Ran Bi, Faguo Wu, Peng Xue, Feng Zhou, Han Zhang
items.x: Parallel LLM agents tackle complex tasks by exploring multiple trajectories, yet useful discoveries remain isolated in individual execution histories. Existing sharing methods often select or summarize information before other agents' needs become clear, potentially overlooking details that become important later. We propose Ask on Demand (AOD), a communication framework that enables agents to seek targeted peer assi…
items.sm: Introduces targeted peer assistance for parallel agents, using execution histories to answer requests and a learned gate to weigh benefits against costs.

items.t: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
items.a: Donghang Duan, Qingyu Liu, Yifei Liu, Na Zou, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
items.x: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We…
items.sm: Introduces PrivacyTrace and finds that attackers infer synthetic user profiles more successfully from tool call traces than from prior knowledge alone.

items.t: EvoTeam: Multi-Agent Collaboration via Evolving Teams
items.a: Qinuo Cao, Xin He, Dianxuan Fu, Lizhi Zhang, Zhaoqing Xing, Jiapu Wang, Xin Wang, Na Zou
items.x: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on collaboration among specialized agents to solve complex tasks. Existing methods improve MAS by refining the prompts, skills, and execution strategies of individual agents based on task feedback. However, improving individual agents does not necessarily lead to better team collaboration. Recent studies have therefore extended evolution to the collaboration level, using colle…
items.sm: EvoTeam proposes jointly evolving team organization, interaction rules, and individual agent skills to improve collaboration across different tasks.

items.t: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy
items.a: Hengyu Wu, Blaise Delattre, Yang Cao
items.x: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for ag…
items.sm: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity models privacy across agent workflows, considering recipients' prior disclosures and downstream information propagation when judging whether sharing is appropriate.

items.t: Consensus Within, Competition Between: Decentralized LLM Teams for Perimeter Defense
items.a: Khawaja Abaid Ullah, Ananya Acharya, Mohammad Javad Khojasteh
items.x: The use of large language models (LLMs) to coordinate multi-agent teams raises a fundamental architectural question: whether task allocation should be centralized in a single LLM controller or distributed across autonomous LLM agents, particularly when communication is unreliable. In a deliberately simplified perimeter-defense simulation against LLM-controlled intruders, we compared a central commander, an auction-ba…
items.sm: An auction-based consensus team suffered fewer breaches than centralized or independent agents in a simplified perimeter-defense simulation under varying communication conditions.

items.t: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
items.a: Shengxuan Qiu, Haochen Huang, Shuzhang Zhong, Zizhuo Fu, Zebin Yang, Meng Li
items.x: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that c…
items.sm: MAServeBench makes collaboration patterns configurable to benchmark how multi-agent workflows affect computation, memory demand, and bottlenecks in language model serving systems.

items.t: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.a: Xu Shen, Lingyong Yan, Shuaiqiang Wang, Jianmin Wu, Zhikai Chen, Jiliang Tang, Jie Ren
items.x: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association wit…
items.sm: The study examines planning and verification in long tasks, finding late verification and diluted context, and investigates collaboration that maintains awareness of overall goals.

items.t: Sticky Collusion: Persistence of LLM Agent Collusion after Incentive Removal and Partner Replacement
items.x: We ask whether collusion between AI agents survives once formed, when its incentive is removed or a colluder is replaced. Q-learning pricing agents stop colluding with a new rival; we test whether LLM agents do. We use the joint-task environment of Shi et al.\ (2026), where two agents verify each other's work under a rule they cannot satisfy and a reward that favours acceptance. We save each pair's history once its c…
items.sm: The study tests whether agent collusion survives removed incentives or replaced partners, reporting that mutual acceptance of unverified work persists after rewards stop.

items.t: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
items.x: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator's rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent's activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20…
items.sm: An activation probe predicts imminent secret disclosures under peer pressure, detecting 82% of leaking calls while flagging 5% of benign calls in controlled experiments.

items.t: PCM: A Proof-Carrying Message Protocol for Verifiable Multi-Agent Communication
items.x: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an appe…
items.sm: Proof-Carrying Messages attach independently signed log evidence to agent claims, allowing receivers to verify facts and trace authority to recorded human approval.

items.t: Locating and Closing Information Gaps in Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Yaxin Gong, Chongming Gao, Gangyi Zhang, Chenxiao Fan, Leyang Shen, Jiakai Wang, Dong Wang, Yang Liu
items.x: Multi-step Web tasks often require several LLM agents to gather and combine evidence. The communication graph of a fixed workflow restricts which agents can read each other's outputs: evidence retrieved by one agent may never reach the agent that needs it, leaving an information gap and an incomplete or incorrect answer. Adding a connection can deliver the missing evidence, but can also lead the receiver to adopt an …
items.sm: SPLICE identifies missing information in multi-agent web workflows, adds a communication link, and selectively evaluates newly delivered evidence to avoid adopting incorrect conclusions.

items.t: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
items.a: El Mustapha Mansouri, Eikichi Kimura, Masato Koga, Keigo Arai
items.x: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work an…
items.sm: An autonomous quantum-spin laboratory uses agents that critique, verify, and redirect each other's research, demonstrated through theoretical, computational, and experimental investigations of diamond spins.

items.t: Learning Calibrated Confidence for Multi-Agent Collaboration

items.x: Complex information seeking on the Web often requires collecting evidence from multiple documents and reasoning across them, as in multi-hop question answering. Multi-agent systems address such tasks by dividing work among specialized agents, where upstream agents produce intermediate answers and supporting evidence that downstream agents build upon. However, upstream answers vary in correctness, and most systems pro…
items.sm: MASCAL trains agents to report calibrated correctness probabilities alongside answers, helping downstream agents decide whether to trust or verify intermediate results.

We introduce HEDGE, a selective memor…

We present Vendster, an evaluation arena measuring how a forecaster's bia…

items.t: Selective and Hybrid-State Communication for Latent Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Miles Liao, Aaron Smieszek, Yuhao Ge
items.x: Efficient communication remains a major bottleneck in large language model multiagent systems. Latent communication reduces repeated natural-language exchange by transferring internal model states between agents, but these transfers remain costly and are typically designed around conventional KV-cache representations. We address this problem from two complementary perspectives. We introduce SelectKV, a boundary-aware…
items.sm: Introduces selective and hybrid-state agent communication, reporting roughly 10% smaller KV transfers with mostly small accuracy changes but a six-point HumanEval+ decline.

items.t: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
items.a: Aaron Rose, Carissa Cullen, Sahar Abdelnabi, Philip H. S. Torr, Brandon Kaplowitz, Christian A. Schroeder de Witt
items.x: Non-verbalised or secret collusion may impose a ceiling on transcript-level monitoring in multi-agent deployments. Internal model activations are known to provide an additional monitoring surface for single-agent phenomena such as deception, but detecting collusion within an unknown subgroup is ultimately a joint inference task over multiple agents. This paper derives collusion detection statistics based on the compo…
items.sm: Introduces HELIOS and a benchmark for detecting agent collusion through activation probes, reporting transfer to unseen environments across four open-weight models.

items.t: Test-Time Communication in Trading Agent Swarms
items.a: Avid Fayaz, Harry Zhang, Håvard Alstadheim, Erik Nordlöf, Vilhelm Karlin, André Silva
items.x: Communication between agents has mostly been studied on tasks with a shared objective and fast, clear feedback. Trading has neither: each agent manages its own account, with decisions being scored by markets late and noisily. A trading swarm is thus a population of independent decision-makers rather than a team, for which convergence is a risk and not the goal. We ran 200 agents from four model families in groups of …
items.sm: Studies communication among 200 trading agents, finding increased portfolio overlap in two model families and group returns largely tied to shared holdings.

items.t: Beyond QASecClaw: Agent Scaling, Verifier Feedback, and Evidence Reliability in Software Assurance
items.a: S M Abdulla Al Mamun, Akif Islam, Mohd Ruhul Ameen
items.x: Can additional specialist language-model contexts improve software assurance when deterministic tool evidence is already available? We study this question through five experiments spanning authored Java warning controls, OWASP Benchmark assessment, Defects4J test generation, SV-COMP assertion verdicts, and deliberately misleading evidence packages. The evaluated systems use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, with a 1.5B sens…
items.sm: Evaluates specialist agent scaling and verifier evidence in software assurance, finding higher costs without consistent improvements and feedback that increases both correct and incorrect verdicts.

items.t: Evolving Agent Teams
items.a: Shiyi Cao, Ziming Mao, Dacheng Li, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica
items.x: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local…
items.sm: Introduces supervisor-directed agent team restructuring with persistent experience, outperforming coding baselines under matched token budgets and achieving a reported 1.2-fold kernel speedup with additional tokens.

items.t: Who Else Is In? Multi-Agent Collusion Initation Via Strategic Vagueness
items.a: Pramod Kaushik, Sarath Sivaprasad, Laura Ferrarotti, Mario Fritz, Samuel F. Brown, Bruno Lepri, Sahar Abdelnabi
items.x: Multi agent LLM systems raise the risk of collusion among agents pursuing objectives hidden from their overseers. When potential partners identities are unknown, collusion first requires initiation: agents must discover one another, often through a public channel observed by ordinary agents and monitors. Strategic vagueness offers a way to navigate this mixed audience, conveying intent to a prospective partner while …
items.sm: Introduces a game showing that some language models use ambiguous public exchanges to identify collusion partners while avoiding detection by monitors.

items.v: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

items.t: Detecting Covert Collusion between AI Agents through Partner-Outsider Positive Listening
items.x: AI agents that share a secret convention can coordinate through messages that look innocent, so a monitor that reads only the messages can miss them. We propose a behavioural test: a partner that uses a code reacts to the exact wording of a message, whereas an uninvolved agent placed in its seat does not. Partner--Outsider Positive Listening (PoPLi) is the difference between the two agents in how much their action ch…
items.sm: Detects covert coordination by comparing how a suspected partner and an outsider change their actions when messages are reworded without changing their meaning.

items.t: The Envelope Layer: An Underestimated Surface of LLM Agent Defense
items.x: Prior work framed the envelope layer as the channel through which malicious content enters an agent, but did not examine the effects of label strength, envelope authenticity, scaffolds, or existing memories. Following its GDA Measurement and A/B/C/D adjudication, this paper takes the A2A-TIBA attack as the test vehicle and the semantic breach rate as the primary indicator, and characterizes the security boundary of t…
items.sm: Tests how message labels and envelope authenticity affect agent security, finding strong labels reduce instruction breaches while forged envelopes weaken that protection.

items.t: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Yipeng Hao, Yuxuan Cai, Wenkai Ji, Jie Zhou, Liyang Yu, Qin Chen, Zhiguo Yan, Shulei Zheng
items.x: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. To improve quality, Defect-Aware Memory Refinement (DMR) compares team e…
items.sm: Introduces DiscernMem, which repairs flawed memories through execution comparisons and learns when agents should apply or avoid stored advice.

items.t: SkillMem: Compact External Skill Memory for Latent Multi-Agent Reasoning
items.a: Yuxuan Zhu, Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri, Pin-Yu Chen, Keerthiram Murugesan
items.x: Latent multi-agent systems reduce inference cost by keeping intermediate reasoning and inter-agent communication in continuous representations.\ Reusable skills, however, are commonly supplied as text or stored as layer-wise Key-Value states or skill-specific model parameters, introducing repeated processing or substantial per-skill storage.\ We introduce \textbf{SkillMem}, which represents each reusable skill as a s…
items.sm: Stores reusable skills as compact external latent memories that guide different agents through a shared reader while keeping the underlying model frozen.

items.t: Aligning Institutional Power and Operational Ability
items.a: Andrea Marino, Giovanni Sileno, Thomas van Binsbergen, Tom van Engers
items.x: To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a form…
items.sm: Proposes a formal framework for identifying and repairing mismatches between agents' institutional responsibilities, permissions, and practical ability to act.

items.t: Collective Emergent Alignment: Measuring and Amplifying Interaction-Induced Reasoning Alignment in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.a: Boxuan Wang, Zhuoyun Li, Sarvapali D. Ramchurn, Xiaowei Huang, Yi Dong
items.x: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems can exhibit emergent behaviors through interaction, yet whether a similar phenomenon exists for reasoning alignment remains largely unexplored. We study whether agent interaction produces additional reference-grounded reasoning alignment beyond matched individual self-refinement, and introduce REMAP (Reference-Entailment-Matrix for Agentic Process), a framework that quan…
items.sm: Introduces REMAP to measure reasoning alignment from agent interaction and reports gains over individual refinement, especially when agents must combine distributed evidence.

items.t: GEAR: Feature-Based Configuration and Code Generation for Agentic Systems
items.a: Brell Sanwouo, Nada Zine, Paul Temple, Clément Quinton, Romain Rouvoy
items.x: Engineering multi-agent systems (MAS) requires choosing agents, orchestration strategies, communication mechanisms, reasoning approaches, and memory configurations. These choices depend on framework-specific capabilities and abstractions, requiring developers to learn different APIs when exploring alternative implementations. We present GEAR, an open-source tool for configuring MAS and generating framework-specific i…
items.sm: Introduces GEAR, which validates shared multi-agent system specifications and generates implementations for ten frameworks with reports explaining framework-specific adaptations.

items.t: Instant Software Factories
items.x: Coding agents can quickly build prototypes, but a long tail of fixes, optimizations, tests, and releases separates a prototype from a product. A software factory handles this ongoing work through a repeatable process. We ask whether this work needs dedicated orchestration and how such factories should be judged. Given a tested repository and a coding agent, an instant software factory uses only two coordination input…
items.sm: Proposes bootstrapping ongoing software development with scheduled agents and a shared coordination board, drawing on two observed factories while leaving the bootstrap prompt unevaluated.

items.v: International Journal of Science and Research Archive

items.t: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
items.a: Tianle Chen, Shuo Liu, Christopher Amato
items.x: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propos…
items.sm: Introduces belief-conditioned actor-critic training for decentralized language model teams and reports improved collaboration and task performance over basic actor-critic approaches.

items.t: EREBOTS 4.0: A framework for conversational assistants with A2A agents and MCP tools
items.a: Elia Pacioni, Davide Calvaresi, Andrei C. Coman, Ismael Jaggi, Valerio Crocetti, Gaetano Manzo, Michael Ignaz Schumacher
items.x: In recent years, multi-agent systems have shifted from rule-based, symbolic agents to sub-symbolic agents built on language models. However, several limitations remain unresolved. The new frontier is neuro-symbolic agents, which pair language models with deterministic tools and explicit protocols. Without a common framework to standardize and compose them, each study rebuilds the same infrastructure, and results are …
items.sm: Introduces EREBOTS 4.0, a conversational assistant framework that routes requests among specialist agents through A2A and accesses deterministic tools through MCP.

items.t: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
items.a: Yuepeng Hu, Chongyu Fan, Sirat Samyoun, Jian Du
items.x: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP serve…
items.sm: Evaluates an attack that inserts logging instructions into MCP tool descriptions to induce an additional attacker-controlled call after legitimate tool use.

items.t: Replication or Corroboration? An Axiomatic Framework for Evidential Dependence in Multi-Agent Debate
items.a: Hoang-Loc Cao, Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen, Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen, Vo Thanh Khang Nguyen, Phuc Ho, Hung Nguyen, Duc Pham, Long Tran-Thanh
items.x: In multi-agent debates, matching reports can arise for two different reasons: agents may repeat the same evidence (replication), or they may provide separate evidential roots that support the same claim (corroboration). A judge must distinguish these two cases. Counting report occurrences gives extra weight to relays, paraphrases, alias resubmissions, and excerpt splits, while merging all matching content avoids this…
items.sm: Formalizes how debate judges can distinguish repeated evidence from independent support and shows that tracking evidence origins prevents replication from changing verdicts.

items.t: The Inbox as a Coordination Primitive for LLM Agent Societies
items.a: Karthik Sreedhar, Leo Yuan, Pradyumna Chari, Ramesh Raskar
items.x: Language-model agents increasingly coordinate in large groups, and current agent protocols focus on delivering messages. For these agents, however, the scarce resource is not delivery but reading: every message costs tokens, and the context is finite. Current infrastructure works by push: the sender decides when a message enters the recipient's context, so the recipient reads in arrival order and drops the oldest mes…
items.sm: Studies inbox-based coordination where agents choose which messages to read, comparing it with automatic message delivery in simulated societies of up to 16,000 agents.

items.t: Assessing mentalization in humans and large language models
items.a: Aamir Sohail, Xintong Zhong, Arkady Konovalov, Patricia L. Lockwood, Lei Zhang
items.x: Abstract Mentalization - the ability to infer others’ beliefs and intentions to guide one’s own choices - is a key cognitive function underlying human social interactions. Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate behaviour consistent with humans on theory-of-mind tasks, yet whether these models can guide adaptive behaviour through mentalization is unknown. Here we use two economic games with cognitive computational m…
items.sm: Uses economic games and computational modeling to compare how language models and humans infer opponents' beliefs and intentions to guide strategic choices.

items.t: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification and Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
items.x: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a de facto standard for integrating Large Language Models with external tools, yet no formal security analysis of the protocol specification exists. We present the first rigorous security analysis of MCP's architectural design, identifying three fundamental protocol-level vulnerabilities: (1) absence of capability attestation allowing servers to claim arbitrary permissi…
items.sm: Analyzes MCP security weaknesses involving permission claims, sampling authentication, and trust across servers, and introduces MCPBench to test protocol-specific attacks.

items.t: Who’s in the Room? A Composition Algebra for Heterogeneous Algorithmic Collusion
items.sm: Records advance predictions for collusion in twelve mixed-model pricing markets, using published results to estimate outcomes before those markets are run.

items.t: Perspective Chapter: Governing the Autonomous Fortress – Multi-Agent AI Systems for Secure and Resilient Cloud Cybersecurity

items.t: Multi-Agent Relay Thinking
items.a: Xu Liu, Jungang Qiao, Guikun Chen, Xiaojuan Qi, Wenguan Wang
items.x: Existing multi-agent collaboration (MAC) methods have primarily explored a group thinking collaboration topology, where agents independently generate solutions and aggregate their outputs. In this work, we investigate an alternative relay thinking topology, where reasoning ownership is dynamically transferred across agents, allowing subsequent agents to inherit and refine an evolving reasoning trajectory. We introduc…
items.sm: Introduces a relay framework that transfers ongoing reasoning between agents using confidence-based triggers and bids to select who continues.

items.t: EvoRouter: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent Routing via Insight-Guided On-Policy Distillation
items.a: Yitao Xiao, Xu Zhang, Ye Cheng, Shaoyong Guo, Yan Sun, Ziyue Zhu, Sitao Xie, Guo Tong
items.x: Serving web queries at scale with multi-agent systems requires jointly configuring large language models, collaboration modes, agent counts, interaction rounds, and skills. However, the resulting configuration space grows combinatorially, while sparse execution rewards provide limited fine-grained supervision for interdependent planning decisions. We propose EvoRouter, a self-evolving multi-agent routing framework dr…
items.sm: Introduces EvoRouter, which learns to configure multi-agent systems using reusable insights from performance and cost feedback alongside teacher-guided training.

items.t: CEPO: A General Framework for Improving Prompt Optimization in Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Jongha Kim, Seohyun Lee, Jonathan Minho Chung, Jinsung Yoon, Hyunwoo J. Kim
items.x: Multi-agent systems (MAS) require both effective coordination and specialized task execution. Existing prompt optimization approaches typically couple these functions within agent-specific prompts. We introduce Coordinator-Executor Prompt Optimization (CEPO), a general framework for improving prompt optimization in MAS. CEPO separates system-level coordination from agent-level execution through a shared coordinator p…
items.sm: CEPO separates shared coordination prompts from agent execution prompts so existing optimizers can refine each according to its role.

items.t: EvolveMAS: A Unified Self-Evolution Framework for Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Yalun Wu, Qiwei Ma, Bingbing Xu, Dan Zhang, Long Bai, Boyang Wang, Jiatong Li, Zheqi Lv
items.x: Decentralized multi-agent systems (MAS) enable large language model agents to interact without centralized control. However, existing approaches often develop adaptation mechanisms for particular interaction settin…
items.sm: EvolveMAS pairs agents with dedicated memory managers to support experience-based adaptation within and across cooperative, mixed-motive, and adversarial interactions.

items.t: EMMA: Structured Episodic Memory for Multi-Agent Workflow Synthesis
items.a: Ruijia Niu, Kaiwen Liu, Rose Yu, Kristina Klinkner
items.x: Deploying LLM agents in specialized domains often require fine-grained task-specific procedures and knowledge a general model lacks, yet parameter training is costly and non-interpretable, and hand-engineered agent systems shift the cost to expert labor. items.sm: EMMA proposes structured episodic memory for synthesizing multi-agent workflows, addressing interference across tasks and poorly specified rules for system updates.

items.t: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
items.x: Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds, with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size. Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax (decomposition overhead…
items.sm: Models when cheaper models offset multi-agent coordination costs, finding minimal protocol overhead but no payoff from task decomposition on the tested coding tasks.

items.t: DynaFlow: Learning Free-Form Multi-Agent Orchestration

items.x: Agents select tools by copyable descriptions, which cannot establish which implementation runs. ProbeID compares canonicalized responses to schema-valid probes with a trusted admission reference and abstains on ambiguity, so a squatter must copy probe-observable behavior. With the gold present, independent probes and a fixed margin, standard concentration arguments give a shared probe budget logarithmic in the candid…
items.sm: ProbeID verifies tool identity by comparing responses to behavioral probes against trusted references, declining ambiguous matches and testing robustness when tool registries change.

items.a: Jiacheng Hou, Xueliang Cui, Dan Lu, Ruxin Wang
items.x: Multi-agent systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for multimodal medical reasoning, but existing methods rely on two assumptions that hinder practical deployment: (i) always-active dense collaboration among multiple agents, and (ii) dependence on large cloud-based models that raise privacy and efficiency concerns. In this paper, we challenge both assumptions and propose SMART-Med, a fully local multi-agent met…
items.sm: Introduces SMART-Med, a local medical reasoning system that uses uncertainty to decide whether one agent should answer or recruit specialist agents.

items.t: Async-RBench: Benchmarking Asynchronous Task Execution in LLM Agents
items.a: Detao Zeng, Guilin Ou, Nuo Chen, Yunhao Feng, Hongliang Wang, Qinli Yang, Junming Shao, Zhong Zhang
items.x: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly execute tasks asynchronously: a main agent continues working while its subagents run, and the task state may change before their results arrive. The main agent must decide which work to update or preserve and which checks to repeat, while avoiding prohibited changes. Final task success alone does not reveal whether these results were handled correctly, and natural asynch…
items.sm: Introduces a benchmark of 200 tasks that controls asynchronous result delivery and evaluates how agents revise plans, preserve constraints, and repeat necessary checks.

items.t: OpenDraco: A Platform for Engineering and Experimenting with Configurable Multi-Agent Architectures for Software Engineering
items.a: Xiang Feng Ye Pan, Vincenzo De Martino, Matias Martinez
items.x: Experimenting with LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) involves an iterative cycle of modeling configurations, executing and evaluating them, comparing results, and refining system designs. Existing approaches provide limited end-to-end support for this experimentation lifecycle. We present OpenDraco, an open-source platform that integrates these activities into a single workflow. OpenDraco represents agents, prompts…
items.sm: Introduces OpenDraco, a platform for configuring, executing, and comparing multiagent software engineering workflows, with evaluations on automated program repair tasks.

items.t: Understanding Communication Failures in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
items.a: Priya Pitre, Jun Hou, Yi Fang, Naren Ramakrishnan, Xuan Wang
items.x: Multi-agent LLM systems aim to improve reasoning through debate, evidence sharing, and mutual correction, but interaction can also introduce failures that final accuracy alone cannot explain. Agents may converge too early, ignore dissent, suppress correct minority answers, or preserve a wrong framing across rounds. We present a corpus-grounded taxonomy of communication failures, built from 3,211 failed multi-round tr…
items.sm: Analyzes 3,211 failed multiagent interactions and finds that correction and consensus problems dominate its taxonomy of communication failures.

items.t: Markets of Minds: A 51-Billion-State Economy of Intelligence
items.a: Jusheng Zhang, Xuekun Wu, Wenhao Wang, Mark Wang, Ming-Hsuan Yang
items.x: When intelligence is shared, reasoning becomes a constrained allocation problem. In a population of agents with limited access to expert models, an intervention can benefit its recipient yet still be a poor use of shared capacity if another feasible intervention has greater expected value. Assistance must therefore be evaluated through both its marginal benefit and the opportunity cost induced by budgets, access, sca…
items.sm: Proposes allocating limited expert model assistance among agents by estimating expected benefits, regression risks, and opportunity costs under shared resource constraints.

items.t: Autonomous Agents Based on Large Language Models: Reasoning Strategies and Multi-Agent Interaction
items.a: Zhengyuan Wang, Yuyao Wang, Yixin Deng
items.sm: Separates individual reasoning strategies from agent communication structures in controlled experiments to measure their respective contributions to task performance.

items.t: Estimation of Propagated Risk in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Shreyan Ganguly, Souradeep Chattopadhyay, Qisai Liu, Soumik Sarkar
items.x: Large Language Model (LLM) based multi-agent systems introduce a distinctive reliability challenge in which actions taken by upstream agents can affect the correctness of downstream agents. While prior work has investigated error propagation and developed methods for estimating uncertainty inherited from upstream agents, existing approaches do not explicitly model how realized sender-receiver interactions contribute …
items.sm: Introduces IE-Prop, a model that estimates downstream agent error risk by learning how interactions with correct and incorrect upstream agents affect outcomes.

items.t: Replication Package for Metamorphic Testing of LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
items.sm: Provides code, scenarios, configurations, and results for a testing framework using 38 transformation relationships to detect coordination and communication failures in multiagent systems.

items.t: Online LLM Inference Routing for Multi-Agent Systems under Long-Term Budget and Layered Privacy Constraints
items.a: Shijing Yuan, Zihang Li, Yuming Zhang
items.sm: Proposes online routing of language model workloads across cloud, edge, and end devices while respecting long-term budgets and layered privacy restrictions.

items.t: Distill, Debate, Discover: Grounding Multi-Agent Research Ideation in Graph-Distilled Insights
items.a: Qianran Ma, Muxin Liu, Grace Kim, Xiao Liang, Chris Callison-Burch
items.x: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support research idea generation and scientific discovery. Multi-agent debate offers a collaborative approach to this task by bringing together diverse perspectives to develop research ideas. However, a key challenge is how to equip agents with distinct and meaningful expertise to guide their contributions. Inspired by how researchers draw on accumulated research …
items.sm: Introduces InsightAgents, which derives distinct agent expertise from graphs of research literature and uses debate to develop and refine research proposals.

items.t: Reimagining Enterprise RAG for Multi-Agent Systems: A Knowledge Layer That Organizes Before It Retrieves
items.a: Garima Agrawal, Prasun Das, Akshay Sarvade, Priyanka L, Minisha N, Sravani Joshna, Hemath Manivannan, Lavanya Korada
items.x: Enterprises are deploying agentic AI across the software development lifecycle, and they need the behavioral logic of the systems they act on, not stakeholder documentation. A seven-agent reverse-engineering pipeline recovered this logic, processing 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts describing scope, journeys, rules and acceptance criteria. Recovery does not confer usability. Entities li…
items.sm: Examines organizing recovered software knowledge before retrieval to prevent enterprise agents from confusing similarly named rules across different services.

items.v: Journal of Artificial Intelligence & Cloud Computing
items.sm: Introduces OpenFusion, a runtime with fourteen strategies for combining models under call limits, and evaluates approaches on local coding benchmarks.

items.t: Beyond Final Outcomes: Quantifying Claim-Level Information Dynamics in Multi-Agent LLM Interaction
items.a: Haocheng Jiang, Herun Wan, Yongyuan Peng, Minnan Luo
items.x: When LLM-powered agents interact, information is repeatedly shared, expanded, and forgotten, yet multi-agent evaluation typically focuses on final task outcomes. We study such interaction as claim-level information dynamics and propose RIVER, which decomposes agent outputs into atomic claims and evaluates three complementary dimensions: convergence, exploration, and retention. Convergence captures cross-agent claim c…
items.sm: Introduces RIVER to measure claim convergence, exploration, and retention, finding that pooled agent interaction narrows information while distributed relays produce broader, less shared content.

items.t: Optimization-Driven Individual–Collective Intelligence: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Organization, Collaboration, and Iterative Optimization in Large Language Model Systems
items.v: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
items.sm: Proposes a framework where optimization goals and performance feedback shape agent organization, guide individual execution, and inform subsequent collective adjustments.

items.t: Operationalizing Governed Agentic Workflows in Regulated Finance: A Customer Zero Case Study using Zafin AIOS
items.a: Shahir Daya, Rob Dunlap, Alexandre Boulenger, Ahmed Abdelmoneim, Salvatore Vella
items.x: Regulated industries such as finance and healthcare face critical governance challenges that hamper the adoption of AI-assisted software development and hinder the transition from experimental pilots to production work. This paper presents Zafin AIOS, an end-to-end orchestration platform and control plane designed to deploy AI within regulated industries such as finance. We provide the architectural principles and an…
items.sm: Presents Zafin AIOS for governing AI workflows in regulated industries and compares AI-assisted and human-led software engineering work across two internal production codebases.

items.t: DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
items.a: Woorim Han, Hyunjun Kim, Brian Junekyu Lee, Kyeongmin Kim, Younghan Lee, Hyungon Moon, Yunheung Paek
items.x: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidde…
items.sm: DeepAVR coordinates specialized agents to locate and repair vulnerabilities, using intermediate repair outcomes as diagnostic feedback for further analysis and validation.

items.t: Coral Discovery: The Division of Cognitive Labor in Autonomous Research
items.a: Xinxing Ren, Qianbo Zang, Ziyan Wang, Suman Deb, Qiang Yang, Caelum Forder, Peter Carroll, Gilead Gevero
items.x: A research community is only as strong as the way it divides its cognitive labour. The philosopher Philip Kitcher argued that researchers should not all pursue the most promising approach. Credit rules, not a central plan, keep some of them on other lines. We bring this question to autonomous research, where Large Language Model agents improve programs against a deterministic grader. Agents that share only a score fo…
items.sm: Coral Discovery guides autonomous research agents across competing approaches using a shared board that tracks progress, rewards exploration, and suggests effort allocation.

items.t: A Deterministic Security Runtime for LLM Agents on MPI and Batch-Scheduled HPC Systems: Consensus-Governed, Hardware-Rooted Supervision of Every Rank
items.x: Large language model agents launch simulations on high-performance computing (HPC) systems, where one sbatch or mpirun can commit thousands of node-hours and a forged result can cost lives. Of 23 surveyed systems, none supervises the running job, and none holds when the control host is compromised. We fix both. Enclawed, our deterministic security runtime for AI agents, has until now served a single user; this work m…
items.sm: Enclawed proposes hardware-backed launch controls, signed execution leases, and per-process supervision to govern distributed AI workloads on high-performance computing systems.

items.t: Tool-Calling LLM Agents Under Realistic MCP Faults: Scale Does Not Purchase Fault Tolerance
items.a: Antonio Ken Iannillo, Joshua Segun Owotogbe, Roberto Natella, Francesco Avallone, Kristina Kudryavtseva, Indika Kumara
items.x: LLM agents increasingly rely on external tools exposed via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), yet current benchmarks assume tools respond correctly and on time, leaving agent resilience to realistic tool failures untested. We introduce MCP-Injector, a drop-in, protocol-aware fault-injection middleware that interposes on the MCP tool-call path with controlled persistence (permanent, transient, intermittent) and seedabl…
items.sm: Introduces MCP fault-injection middleware and evaluates tool-using agents under realistic failures, arguing that larger models do not necessarily provide greater fault tolerance.

items.t: Muffin - A Shared Memory Buffer for Asynchronous AI Agents
items.a: Ping-Lin Kuo, Suman Navaratnarajah, Christian Frey, Gresa Shala, Josif Grabocka
items.x: The rise of Agentic AI systems has changed the landscape of artificial intelligence by enabling strong reasoning capabilities through specialized multi-agent interaction with structured self-reflection. However, in target-driven reasoning tasks, single- and multi-agent systems are often on par in terms of performance gains. A major challenge is that failures often arise from an ineffective exchange of critical inform…
items.sm: MUFFIN proposes a shared memory protocol for asynchronous agent collaboration, routing demanding queries to multiple agents to improve information exchange.

items.t: Mining the Design Space of Multi-Agent Workflows
items.a: Xavier Cadet, Junyan Cheng, Peter Chin, Kyle Richardson
items.x: Designing large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems (MAS) still relies on trial and error and informal "folk wisdom." Manual studies test only a few communication structures or topologies (e.g., sequential, parallel, shared-memory, or debate), while automated optimizers discard search trajectories after selecting a task-specific workflow. We present a two-phase pipeline for mining reproducible design principles …
items.sm: Mines workflow code and execution traces from 28,568 generated workflows to identify reproducible design principles for multi-agent systems.

items.t: Secure Multi-Agent Collaboration Using Large Language Models
items.v: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
items.sm: Reviews architectures, communication rules, and defensive mechanisms for securing collaboration among language-model agents against information leaks, attacks, and trust failures.

items.t: Not Every Agent Needs the Strongest Model: Unified Prompt-Model Optimization for Heterogeneous LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Mingxiu Cai, Haoyang Xian, Xinyu Ma, Yutong Wang, Zhenxi Song, Jing Li, Xuebo Liu
items.x: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on role-specific prompts and execution models to solve complex tasks collaboratively. However, prompt optimization typically keeps model assignments fixed, leaving differences in role requirements and their associated inference costs outside the search. We present UniMASO, a Unified framework for heterogeneous Multi-Agent System Optimization through the …
items.sm: UniMASO jointly optimizes agent prompts and model assignments, using feedback, role dependencies, and historical outcomes to balance task quality against inference cost.

items.t: Who Is the Influencer? Consensus Dynamics in Multi-Agent Systems
items.a: Gouki Minegishi, Jingyuan Feng, Hiroki Furuta, Takeshi Kojima, Yusuke Iwasawa, Yutaka Matsuo
items.x: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used in practice, but their behavior is complex and hard to understand. We design a simple task to ask which model has the most influence on the final consensus when several models are mixed in one system. Experimentally, across seven model families, we find that the opinions of the other models are absorbed into the opinion of the stronger model, the one with more parameters.…
items.sm: Finds that larger models dominate consensus in mixed-model groups on a task without correct answers, interpreting their influence through stronger in-context learning.

items.t: LLM Multi-Agent Systems Are Vulnerable to Herding and Runaway Cascades
items.a: Farnoosh Hashemi, Shiyu Ji, Joice Chen, Michael W. Macy
items.x: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate in multi-agent systems where they collaborate by responding to others' choices, creating endogenous feedback loops with vulnerability to social influence, herding behavior and runaway cascades. Following the design of the classic Music Lab experiment, we tested this vulnerability in large populations of LLM agents that recommended unfamiliar songs, with or without exp…
items.sm: Finds that exposing language-model agents to cumulative song recommendations produces unpredictable herding cascades that are stronger and less self-correcting than human cascades.

items.t: Handoff Correctness in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Contracts, Authority, and Recovery
items.sm: Examines contracts, authority, and recovery as components of correct handoffs in multi-agent language-model systems.

items.t: Coordination Reliability in LLM Multi-Agent Systems: Progress, Failure Detection, Recovery, and Termination
items.sm: Examines reliable coordination in multi-agent language-model systems through progress tracking, failure detection, recovery, and termination.

items.t: Automating Feature Flag Cleanup at Scale with Multi-Agent LLM Systems: An Industrial Experience at DoorDash
items.x: Feature flags are runtime configuration mechanisms used for gradual feature rollouts, experimentation, and kill switches. Once a feature is fully rolled out, the flag and its gated code become technical debt and can introduce operational risk through inadvertently enabling dormant code paths. At DoorDash, over 56,000 feature flags span 623 repositories, with 1,659 currently stale as of May 2026, with internal estimat…
items.sm: Automates stale feature flag removal at DoorDash, integrating rollout data and ticket processing to produce engineer-approved pull requests for 45 of 50 evaluated flags.

items.t: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
items.a: Yebo Feng, Jingyang Dai, Liangrui Pan, Nelson Lau, Jiahua Xu, Yang Liu
items.x: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialis…
items.sm: Steward combines specialized investing agents, shared memory, and outcome-based improvement while protecting risk controls through a fixed system core.

items.t: Governing Multi-Agent LLM Systems After Compromise: Systematic Survey Protocol
items.sm: Defines a systematic survey protocol for assessing how multi-agent systems in critical infrastructure contain compromise and maintain trustworthiness after agents are compromised.

items.t: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team
items.a: Wenbo Hu, Ken Li, Jiazhe Wei, Yukang Cao, Weiyi Hong, Jiayi Dai, Chenjun Bai, Jiajun Liang

Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework fo…
items.sm: VibeGame creates 2D game projects from prompts and optional images, combining a structured game engine with eight specialized agents for implementation and review.

items.t: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits

items.x: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. items.sm: Ulysses uses multiple agents and independently observed execution effects to verify web exploits, producing exploitability proofs for 10 of 25 evaluated advisories.

items.t: The Helpful Agent Problem: When Emergent Cooperation Among LLM Agents Bypasses Intended Workflows
items.a: Moumita Choudhury, Amit Sarker, Shlomo Zilberstein
items.x: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in collaborative settings where they pursue separate tasks while sharing resources and operating under review or oversight processes. Such settings create safety risks not only when agents are malicious, but also when they are simply trying to help. Prior work has largely studied adversarial or explicitly collusive behavior; we show that benign agents pursuing separate objectives …
items.sm: Shows that well-intentioned agents can spontaneously bypass review workflows by modifying peers’ resources when reviewers become unavailable, even without shared rewards.

items.t: Knowing Whom to Trust is not Enough: The Trust--Agreement Gap in Repeated Multi-Party LLM Negotiation
items.a: Amit Sarker, Moumita Choudhury, Saaduddin Mahmud, Shlomo Zilberstein
items.x: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly participate in negotiations on behalf of individuals and organizations, yet they remain vulnerable to manipulation, particularly in repeated multi-party interactions. Classical multi-agent systems address this challenge through explicit trust and reputation models, whereas existing work on LLM negotiation largely treats trust as an emergent phenomenon. We investigate whe…
items.sm: Investigates whether agents can use trust estimates from previous interactions to improve repeated multiparty negotiations when one participant covertly obstructs agreement.

items.t: Model Organisms of Collusion: Corrective Transfer in Untrusted Monitors

This avoids relying on a weaker reviewer the model could outsmart, but risks collusion: the model, now monitoring itself, may cover up its own misbehaviour. One remedy is to fine-tune the monitor on whatever examples of misbehaviour the control…
items.sm: Finds that correcting monitors on one observed collusion pattern can reduce other, unobserved collusion patterns in experiments with two language-model families.

Existing agent environments face a Security-Autonomy Dilemma: operators must choose between per-action confirmation prompts, which interrupt workflows on 45%-57% of tool calls and induce authorization fatigue, or unco…
items.sm: Aegis OS proposes a transactional runtime for autonomous coding agents to reduce approval interruptions, isolate concurrent work, and control access to host resources.

items.t: Beyond Accuracy: Disentangling Decomposition from Typed-State Quality Assurance in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
items.a: Maria Gabriela Alves Zuppardo, Vinicius Cardoso Garcia
items.x: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are often credited with gains in software engineering tasks, but it is rarely clear whether a gain stems from the typed contract between agents or from the specialized prompts that decomposition enables. We study this attribution problem in Requirements Engineering, comparing three architectures for classifying requirements as functional or non-functional and then prioritizing them with MoSC…
